01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
redacted
With private details removed or hidden.
beneficiary
A person receiving a benefit.
conditional on
Dependent upon a requirement being met.
authenticate
Confirm that a document is genuine.
issued notice
A decision letter sent or given officially.
reconstruct
Work out something from surviving pieces of information.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Helen Ward contacted Emma two days after their first conversation. She had consulted her cousin, who preferred not to speak to a journalist but was willing for Helen to show a redacted copy of the foundation's 2011 letter. The permission was limited to reading it in a private meeting. It did not include photographing, copying or publishing the document.

Emma repeated those conditions when Helen arrived. Sarah joined them only after Helen agreed. The paper was folded and bore the Glenarraidh Education Trust's name and a date in September 2011. Emma treated those features as details to verify, not proof that the document was genuine.

The wording was significant. It described the cousin's application as selected for travel support, then explained that payment was conditional on evidence of course enrolment and confirmed travel costs. It did not state that funds had been transferred.

“Then the student was a beneficiary,” Sarah suggested.

“A selected applicant,” Emma corrected. “We don't yet know whether the conditions were met or any payment followed.”

The letter also contained a paragraph on the fourteen-day review procedure for unsuccessful applicants. Its wording resembled the blank template that Fiona Bell had previously supplied. That similarity suggested a possible connection between the template and an issued notice, but did not authenticate either copy or show how consistently the wording had been used.

Emma asked Helen when her cousin had received the decision. Helen could not remember. She recalled helping to complete the application, but had found the letter much later with family paperwork. The date printed at its head was not evidence of delivery on that day.

She also asked whether Helen knew of any appeal. Helen shook her head. Her cousin had apparently been selected, and Helen knew nothing about other applicants. Emma deliberately avoided inviting guesses about students whose details Helen had never seen.

Throughout the meeting, Emma took brief notes within the limits Helen had agreed. No recording was made, and she did not retain an image of the paper. Before leaving, Helen offered to ask her cousin whether a redacted copy could later be provided for examination. That decision remained the cousin's.

Emma returned to the original newspaper report: eight students reportedly selected, followed by a correction that gave no replacement figure. Even if the letter proved authentic, it would establish at most one case of selection. A total could not be reconstructed from a single example, and selection still did not equal payment.

In her notebook, she drew two boxes: What the letter says and What has been verified. They did not yet contain the same information. It was progress, but of the careful kind.
